title: How to File ITR-2 for RSUs: A Schedule-by-Schedule Guide
summary: A schedule-by-schedule guide to filing ITR-2 with foreign RSUs: Schedule S, CG, FA, FSI and TR, with one worked example in rupees.
body_markdown:
If your RSUs from a foreign employer vested or were sold during the year, the numbers go into six schedules of ITR-2: Schedule S, Schedule CG, Schedule OS, Schedule FA, Schedule FSI and Schedule TR. This guide walks through them in the order you will fill them, with one example carried all the way through.


It follows the ITR-2 that[CBDT notified for AY 2026-27](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/sites/default/files/2026-04/Notification%20No.46_2026.pdf) , which is the form for income of FY 2025-26. A belated return for that year can be filed until 31 December 2026, and a return already filed can be revised until 31 March 2027.


If you are still deciding which form applies to you or what has to be reported at all, start with[ITR for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/itr-for-rsu-holders) . For how the tax itself is calculated, read[how foreign RSUs are taxed in India](https://paasa.com/blog/how-rsus-are-taxed-in-india) .

## What to keep ready before you start


Most of the time spent on this return goes into finding numbers, not typing them. Collect these first.


Document What you take from it


Form 16 and Form 12BA from your employer The rupee perquisite for the shares that vested, and the TDS on it


Form 26AS and AIS from the e-filing portal A cross-check of salary, TDS and any other income already reported against your PAN


Vesting confirmations from your stock plan account Vest date, shares vested, FMV per share, shares sold to cover tax


Trade confirmations or the realised gain/loss report Sale date, shares sold and sale price for every sale, including sell-to-cover


Dividend statement or Form 1042-S Gross dividend and US tax withheld


Calendar-year account statement (January to December) Holdings and values for Schedule FA


SBI TT buying rates for the dates you need Conversion of every dollar figure into rupees


If your records are scattered,[how to keep records for RSU tax calculations](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-keep-records-for-rsu-tax-calculations) shows where each of these sits in a stock plan account.


## The example used in this walkthrough


**Example.** Suppose you are a product manager in Hyderabad, resident and ordinarily resident in India, and your employer is listed in the US. In FY 2025-26 one tranche of RSUs vests, your employer sells some shares to cover the tax, you receive a dividend and you sell a few more shares in February. The exchange rates are illustrative, set close to where SBI's TT buying rate stood on those dates.


Event Exchange rate used Rupee value


12 August 2025: 40 shares vest at an FMV of $150 ₹87.00 (31 July 2025) Perquisite of ₹5,22,000, or ₹13,050 per share


12 August 2025: 14 shares sold to cover tax at $150.50 ₹87.00 (31 July 2025) Sale proceeds of ₹1,83,309


15 December 2025: dividend of $15.60 on 26 shares, US tax withheld $3.90 ₹89.00 (30 November 2025) Dividend of ₹1,388, US tax of ₹347


16 February 2026: 10 shares sold at $172 ₹91.00 (31 January 2026) Sale proceeds of ₹1,56,520


**Shares still held on 31 March 2026** **Cost fixed at vesting** **16 shares with a cost of ₹2,08,800**


### The result: four sets of numbers to carry into ITR-2


You are taxed on all 40 shares at vesting but receive 26, because 14 were sold to pay the tax. The perquisite, the two sales, the dividend and the year-end holding each go into a different schedule, and the steps below place them one by one.


Every conversion uses SBI's TT buying rate on the last day of the month before the event. That was Rule 115 for FY 2025-26 and is now[Rule 206](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/rule-206-1) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026, with the same method. Schedule FA is the one exception, and Step 5 covers it.


## Step 1: Start the return and choose your schedules


Log in to the income tax e-filing portal, start a return for the assessment year you are filing for and choose ITR-2. You can fill it online or in the offline utility; the schedules are the same in both.


You fill only the schedules that apply to you. An RSU holder with the events in our example needs Schedule S, Schedule CG, Schedule OS, Schedule FA, Schedule FSI and Schedule TR, along with the general information, deductions and tax paid sections that every return has.


Two answers matter for RSU holders. Your residential status, in the general information part, decides whether Schedule FA applies at all, since it is required only from those who are resident and ordinarily resident. The form also asks whether you held any asset outside India or had income from a source outside India during the year, and vested shares of a foreign company mean the answer is yes.


## Step 2: Schedule S, the vesting perquisite


Schedule S holds your salary, employer by employer. Its first block splits gross salary into three rows: salary as per section 17(1), value of perquisites as per section 17(2), and profits in lieu of salary as per section 17(3).


The RSU perquisite belongs on the perquisites row. For FY 2025-26 the charging provision is section 17(2)(vi) of the 1961 Act, which becomes section 17(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27.


### What to enter


- The employer's name and TAN, as they appear on Form 16.
- Salary as per section 17(1) from Part B of Form 16.
- Value of perquisites from Part B of Form 16, which already includes the RSU perquisite along with any other perquisites.


In the example, ₹5,22,000 of the perquisites figure comes from the August vest. Do not recompute it if it differs slightly from your own working. The figure in Form 16 is what your employer reported and deducted tax on, and it is also your cost of acquisition for the shares.


If the perquisite is missing from Form 16 altogether, it still has to be reported here. Read[how to read your Form 16 when you have RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/form-16-rsu-holders) before you go further.


## Step 3: Schedule CG, every sale including sell-to-cover


Schedule CG has a short-term part (A) and a long-term part (B), each divided by type of asset. Shares listed only on a foreign exchange do not fit the rows meant for Indian listed equity on which securities transaction tax is paid.


- **Held for 24 months or less from the vest date:** short-term, entered under item A5, "From sale of assets other than at A1 or A2 or A3 or A4 above".
- **Held for more than 24 months from the vest date:** long-term, entered under item B8, "From sale of assets where B1 to B7 above are not applicable".


Both items ask for the same things: the full value of consideration, the cost of acquisition without indexation, the cost of improvement, and expenditure wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer. The form then works out the gain.


### What to enter


- **Full value of consideration:** the sale proceeds in rupees, converted at SBI's TT buying rate on the last day of the month before the month of sale.
- **Cost of acquisition:** the per-share perquisite value from vesting, multiplied by the shares sold. It is already in rupees and is not converted again.
- **Expenditure on transfer:** brokerage or commission charged on the sale, converted the same way as the proceeds.


The shares sold to cover tax at vesting are a sale in your name, so they go here as well. This entry is easy to miss, because the sale never shows up in Form 16.


Row in item A5 Sell-to-cover sale (14 shares) February sale (10 shares) Total you enter


Full value of consideration ₹1,83,309 ₹1,56,520 ₹3,39,829


Cost of acquisition without indexation ₹1,82,700 ₹1,30,500 ₹3,13,200


**Short-term capital gain** **₹609** **₹26,020** **₹26,629**


### The result: ₹26,629 of short-term gain, of which ₹609 comes from the sell-to-cover sale


The items take totals for the year, so work out each sale separately and keep that working with your records. If some of your sales are long-term and some are short-term, the long-term ones go to item B8 and are taxed at 12.5%.


Further down, Schedule CG has a table for the dates on which the gains arose, split into the advance tax quarters. The ₹609 goes in the 16 June to 15 September column and the ₹26,020 in the 16 December to 15 March column, on the row for short-term gains taxable at applicable rates. The return uses this table to work out interest on any advance tax shortfall, so do not leave it blank.


If the year ended in a net capital loss, it is carried forward only when the return is filed by the original due date. For the rates, set-off rules and lot-wise working, read[capital gains tax on RSU shares](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) .


## Step 4: Schedule OS, dividends


Dividends from your employer's shares are income from other sources. In Schedule OS they go under gross dividends, on the general row for dividend income.


Enter the gross dividend in rupees, before the US tax withheld. In the example that is ₹1,388, not the ₹1,041 that reached the account. Schedule OS also has a table for the quarter in which the income arose; a dividend paid on 15 December falls in the 16 September to 15 December column.


If your shares paid no dividend during the year, skip this step and Step 7, and fill only the capital gains row in Step 6.


## Step 5: Schedule FA, the account and the shares


Schedule FA is a disclosure of what you held abroad, and it runs on the calendar year. For the AY 2026-27 return, it covers 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2025, so the February 2026 sale in our example does not appear in it this year.


RSU holders fill two tables. Table A2 is for the foreign custodial account, which is the stock plan or brokerage account that holds the shares. Table A3 is for the foreign equity itself, with each vesting tranche on its own line.


### Table A2: the account


Table A2 asks for the country, the name, address and ZIP code of the financial institution, your account number, your status as owner, the account opening date, the peak balance during the period, the closing balance, and the gross amount paid or credited to the account, with its nature chosen from interest, dividend, sale proceeds or other income.


### Table A3: the shares


Table A3 asks for the country, the name, address and ZIP code of the entity, the nature of the entity, the date of acquiring the interest, the initial value of the investment, the peak value during the period, the closing value, the total gross amount paid or credited on the holding, and the total gross proceeds from sale or redemption during the period.


Schedule FA does not use the month-end rate from the other schedules. Under the department's[step-by-step guide to Schedules FSI, TR and FA](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/sites/default/files/2026-03/Step%20by%20Step%20Guide%20FA%20FSI.pdf) , each value is converted at SBI's TT buying rate on its own date: the initial value at the rate on the date of investment, the peak value at the rate on the date of the peak, and the closing value and the income and sale proceeds at the rate on 31 December.


The tranche line covers all 40 shares, because the heading of Table A3 covers foreign equity held at any time during the calendar year. In the example, the statement shows all 40 shares delivered to the account before 14 were sold to cover the tax, so you held them and the sale goes under gross proceeds. If your employer had withheld those 14 shares before delivery, there would be nothing to report for them, and the line would cover only the 26 shares you received.


Table A3 column Entry for the August 2025 tranche How it is worked out


Date of acquiring the interest 12 August 2025 The vest date


Initial value of the investment ₹5,24,400 40 × $150 × ₹87.40, the rate on the vest date


Peak value of investment during the period ₹5,24,400 Highest on the vest date, when all 40 shares were held, since the 26 shares left never reached that value in 2025


Closing value ₹3,95,457 26 × $170 × ₹89.47, the price and rate on 31 December 2025


Total gross amount paid or credited ₹1,396 $15.60 dividend × ₹89.47


**Total gross proceeds from sale** **₹1,88,513** **14 × $150.50 × ₹89.47, the sell-to-cover sale**


### The result: one line in Table A3 for the tranche, and one line in Table A2 for the account


The rupee figures here differ a little from those in Schedule S, Schedule CG and Schedule OS. That is expected, because Schedule FA converts on its own dates and reports no tax.


If your total income is above ₹1 crore, the shares you still hold on 31 March also go in Schedule AL, at cost, under shares and securities. Unvested RSUs are not reported in either schedule. For the peak value method, several tranches and shares sold during the year, read[Schedule FA for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/schedule-fa-rsu-holders) .


## Step 6: Schedule FSI, income from outside India


Schedule FSI lists the income you earned from sources outside India, country by country, and it is available only to residents. The income must already be included under its own head in the return; Schedule FSI repeats it so that the foreign tax credit can be computed.


For each country, the schedule asks for the country code, your taxpayer identification number in that country, and then, for each head of income, the income from outside India, the tax paid outside India, the tax payable on that income in India, the tax relief available and the relevant article of the tax treaty.


### What to enter


- **Country:** the United States, for shares of a US-listed company.
- **Taxpayer identification number:** your tax identification number in that country. The department's guide says to enter your passport number if that country has not allotted you one.
- **Other sources row:** the gross dividend of ₹1,388 and the US tax of ₹347, with Article 10 of the India-US tax treaty as the relevant article.
- **Capital gains row:** the ₹26,629 of gains on the US shares, with nil tax paid outside India.


The relief on each row is the lower of the tax paid abroad and the Indian tax on that income. At the 30% slab the Indian tax on the dividend is higher than ₹347, so the full ₹347 is available as credit. The perquisite from vesting is salary earned for work in India, so it does not go in Schedule FSI.


## Step 7: Schedule TR and Form 67, the foreign tax credit


Schedule TR is a one-line summary of Schedule FSI for each country. It shows the country code, your taxpayer identification number, the total tax paid outside India, the total tax relief available and the section under which the relief is claimed. For the US, which has a tax treaty with India, the section is 90.


In the example, the total tax paid outside India and the total relief are both ₹347. The schedule also asks whether any foreign tax on which you claimed relief was later refunded to you by the foreign tax authority, which will normally be no.


The credit is allowed only if you also file Form 67 on the e-filing portal, with the same income and tax figures and proof of the tax withheld. File it before you submit the return, so that the credit is on record when the return is processed. From Tax Year 2026-27, Form 67 is replaced by Form 44. Read the[Form 67 guide](https://paasa.com/blog/form-67-guide-for-indian-investors) for the form itself.


## Step 8: Check the tax paid, then submit and verify


The tax paid section has a table for TDS on salary. Check that the TDS against your employer's TAN matches Part A of Form 16 and Form 26AS, since the tax paid through sell-to-cover reaches the government as salary TDS.


Then review the computation. TDS on the perquisite does not cover capital gains or dividends, so a balance is often payable at this stage, along with interest if advance tax fell short during the year. Read[advance tax for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/advance-tax-rsu-holders) to avoid that next year.


Pay any balance, preview the return, submit it and complete the e-verification.


## Common mistakes on the form


- **Leaving the sell-to-cover sale out of Schedule CG.** The gain is small, but the sale is yours and the proceeds appear in your broker's records.
- **Entering the amount received as the dividend.** Schedule OS and Schedule FSI take the gross dividend, and the US tax is claimed separately as credit.
- **Using financial-year holdings in Schedule FA.** The schedule covers January to December and converts each value on its own date.
- **Filling Table A3 but not Table A2.** The shares and the account that holds them are separate disclosures.
- **Claiming credit in Schedule TR without Form 67.** The claim in the return needs the form behind it.
- **Using the cost shown by the broker.** Your cost is the rupee perquisite from Form 16, not the dollar cost basis on a US statement.
